analysis.one_liner: Charges royalties on natural gas companies vent, flare, or leak from federal and offshore leases.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in August 2026 with three cosponsors and referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, which took no further action before the session ended in January 2027.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies drilling on public land and offshore leases currently pay royalties only on the natural gas they sell. Gas that is vented into the air, burned off in flares, or leaks out of equipment is currently free. This bill would require royalty payments on that wasted gas too, for new leases, with narrow exceptions for emergencies and gas used on the lease itself. That gives companies a direct financial reason to capture gas instead of releasing it, and methane — the main ingredient of natural gas — is a powerful heat-trapping gas that drives climate change.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people benefit twice: taxpayers collect royalties on gas that now escapes for free, and the public gets less methane pollution. Methane is a greenhouse gas far more potent than carbon dioxide in the near term, so cutting leaks and flaring from federal lands reduces the pace of climate change and associated costs like extreme weather and air-quality problems. The bill also locks in a 2024 rule from the Bureau of Land Management designed to prevent waste of gas on federal leases.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and people breathing cleaner air

how_it_helps.text: For new federal and outer continental shelf leases, royalties must be assessed on all gas produced, including gas lost to venting, flaring, or negligent leaks, giving companies a price signal to capture gas instead of releasing it [S2].

The bill directs the Bureau of Land Management to enforce its April 2024 waste-prevention rule and forbids finalizing a weaker June 2026 proposed replacement unless the replacement demonstrably cuts waste further or improves public health [S2].
Narrow exceptions keep the requirement workable: gas vented or flared for up to 48 hours in a genuine emergency, gas used on the lease itself, and unavoidably lost gas are exempt [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies operating on federal land and offshore leases. They would pay royalties on gas they currently vent, flare, or lose for free on new leases, which creates a financial incentive to invest in capture equipment rather than let gas escape.

drawbacks.text: Critics argue charging royalties on vented and flared gas raises drilling costs, which can reduce production and be passed to consumers through higher energy prices, and that some waste events are unavoidable and hard to meter accurately [S2].
The requirement applies only to leases issued after enactment, so a large share of existing federal production keeps operating under current rules for years [S2].
The bill fixes federal land royalties on wasted gas but does not by itself limit emissions from oil and gas produced on private or state land, so most national methane emissions are untouched [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is favorable to the public: companies pay for gas they currently waste for free, which both raises public revenue and discourages a potent greenhouse gas. The exemptions for emergencies and unavoidable losses acknowledge real-world limits. The main honest caveats are that it only covers new leases, costs may partly reach consumers, and the bill leaves the broader, larger share of methane emissions from non-federal production untouched.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee in August 2026 and the committee has taken no action on it with the session ending January 3, 2027.

narrative.text: Rep. Luz Rivas introduced the Methane Pollution Accountability Act on August 6, 2026, with Reps. Huffman and Norton as original cosponsors [S1][S2].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources the same day, and the action history shows no hearing, markup, or floor vote [S4].
Three Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did [S3].

The bill would prevent the Bureau of Land Management from finalizing a June 2026 proposed rule that would revise its 2024 waste-prevention rule, unless the replacement provably reduces waste or improves public health [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies drilling on federal land keep paying nothing for gas they vent, flare, or leak, and taxpayers forgo the royalties the bill would collect on new leases.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas companies drilling on federal land

sides.party_line_note: All three cosponsors are Democrats and no Republican joined, but no vote was ever held, so the chamber's actual split was never recorded.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers on federal and offshore leases
industries.note: The bill requires royalty payments on gas they currently vent, flare, or lose for free on new leases, ending a form of uncompensated waste. The industry's savings from venting come directly out of taxpayer revenue and cleaner air, so its interest in the status quo runs against the public's.

industries.industry: Bureau of Land Management rulemaking (federal royalty administration)
industries.note: The bill blocks the June 2026 proposed replacement of the 2024 waste-prevention rule unless it demonstrably cuts waste further, limiting the agency's flexibility. It preserves the stronger existing rule in place.

analysis.trajectory: With no committee action, three cosponsors, and under five months left in the session, the bill will almost certainly expire at the end of the 119th Congress without a hearing or vote; its prospects would require a new introduction in the next Congress.
